messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 45-year-old European American journalist, has been struggling with symptoms that began shortly after his captivity experience. During those harrowing weeks in captivity, he was subjected to intense physical and psychological torture, which left deep emotional and physical scars. Since his release, Mark’s memories of the traumatic event have become overwhelming. His mind is plagued by vivid replays of the frightening moments, like a film that plays over and over again. These memories force their way into his consciousness without warning, especially when he encounters certain triggers. For example, any neck pain immediately transports him back to the painful sensations he felt during those torturous sessions. When he smells alcohol, which was used as part of the torture process, Mark’s mind is flooded with distressing images that bring back the same terror he experienced at the time. Mark has developed a high level of hypervigilance and reacts strongly to any unexpected or loud sounds, often interpreting them as immediate threats. This heightened state of alertness has led to frequent false alarms where he believes he is in danger even when there is no real threat. His hypervigilant state exacerbates his memories; every time he hears a sudden noise, it triggers the same overwhelming sense of fear and trauma that he experienced during captivity. Consequently, these heightened states often lead to a resurgence of painful memories. His occupation as a journalist adds another layer of difficulty. Working in an environment where he is frequently exposed to various sounds and physical interactions has made his condition more challenging. Mark’s colleagues have noticed that he reacts strongly when they accidentally touch him or work too closely together, leading to strained professional relationships. His wife also observes the tension at home, particularly during social gatherings where the smell of alcohol can set off a series of flashbacks. Mark’s hypervigilance has become a self-reinforcing cycle. The more he is on high alert, the more likely he is to experience false alarms, which in turn intensify his intrusive memories and trigger reactions like neck pain or panic at the sound of unexpected noises. This constant state of fear and reliving trauma has significantly impacted his ability to function both professionally and personally. The relentless cycle of hypervigilance leading to memory intrusions and subsequent triggering sensations has become overwhelming for Mark. He finally sought help when he realized that these symptoms were not only affecting him but also causing strain in his relationships with colleagues and family members. What frightens him most is the fear of never fully recovering from this traumatic experience, while what he hopes for is a way to regain control over his life and find peace without the constant specter of trauma looming over every moment.
